passages.title: Two Chairs by the Window
passages.passage:
When my family moved to Da Nang, I was eleven and certain that I would never make another friend. My old school was five hundred kilometres away, and my best friend, Linh, had promised to write every week. She kept her promise for about a month. After that, the letters became shorter, and then they stopped. I did not blame her. She had a new class, a new football team and, I supposed, new friends.

The girl who sat next to me in my new school was called Mai. She did not say much at first. In fact, for the whole of the first term, our conversations were mostly about borrowing pens. Then one rainy afternoon, when the buses were late, we sat on two plastic chairs by the classroom window and talked for an hour. I discovered that she collected old stamps, that she was afraid of dogs, and that she had also moved schools, twice. By the end of the year, we were doing homework at each other's houses.

People sometimes say that a true friend is someone you can be silent with. I think that is only half the story. Mai and I could be silent together, but we could also argue, and the arguments never lasted. Once, we did not speak for three days after a disagreement about a school project. On the fourth day, she left a stamp from Brazil on my desk. Neither of us mentioned the argument again.

I am fifteen now, and Linh and I still send each other a message on our birthdays. I do not think of her as a lost friend, just a friend from another chapter. What the last four years have taught me is that friendship does not depend on how long you have known someone. It depends on whether both people are willing to sit down on those two chairs and keep talking.

questions.q: What is the passage mainly about?
options: Why the writer's old friend stopped writing letters
How the writer came to understand what keeps a friendship alive
The difficulties of moving to a new city at the age of eleven
Why silence is the true test of a friendship
questions.explanation: Every paragraph builds towards the final lesson: friendship depends on both people being willing to keep talking. Linh's letters and the move are details, and the writer says silence is only half the story.

questions.q: According to the first paragraph, why did Linh's letters stop?
options: She was angry that the writer had moved away.
The distance was too great for letters to arrive.
She had become busy with her new life.
The writer stopped replying to them.
questions.explanation: The writer does not blame Linh because she had a new class, a new team and, probably, new friends — in other words, a new life. Nothing suggests anger or a problem with the post.

questions.q: What can be inferred about Mai during the first term?
options: She disliked the writer and avoided her.
She was quiet and took time to open up.
She never brought her own pens to school.
She was often absent from class.
questions.explanation: Mai 'did not say much at first' and the two only talked about pens until a rainy afternoon changed things. That points to shyness, not dislike — later they became close friends.

questions.q: The word 'chapter' in the last paragraph is closest in meaning to
options: a section of a book
a period of someone's life
a school year
a distant town
questions.explanation: 'A friend from another chapter' means a friend from an earlier period of the writer's life. The literal book meaning does not fit the context.

questions.q: In paragraph 3, 'that' in 'I think that is only half the story' refers to
options: the writer's friendship with Mai
the saying that a true friend is someone you can be silent with
the fact that arguments never lasted
the disagreement about a school project
questions.explanation: 'That' points back to the sentence just before it — the popular saying about silence. The writer then adds the other half: real friends can also argue and recover.

questions.q: Mai had changed schools more times than the writer.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: The only school change the writer describes is the one move to Da Nang, while Mai had also moved schools, twice. The word also invites the comparison: two moves against one, so the statement is True.

questions.q: The writer and Linh have met in person since the move to Da Nang.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: We are only told that they exchange birthday messages. The passage says nothing about whether they have ever met again, so the answer is Not Given.

passages.title: Jobs That Did Not Have Names
passages.passage:
Ask your grandparents what they wanted to be when they were fifteen, and you will probably hear a short list: teacher, doctor, farmer, soldier, shopkeeper. Ask a fifteen-year-old today and the list is longer and stranger. Some want to be game designers, drone pilots or online video makers. Twenty years ago, most of those jobs did not even have names.

Careers advisers say this change is happening faster than ever. A report from a Vietnamese employment website last year found that nearly a third of the jobs advertised in Ho Chi Minh City did not exist in the same form in 2010. Many of them are connected to technology, but not all. Delivery riders, for example, have become a common sight in every city, and their work depends on a phone app that was invented only a few years ago.

For students, this can sound worrying. How can you prepare for a job that has not been invented yet? Nguyen Thi Hoa, who advises secondary-school students in Hanoi, tells them not to panic. "Nobody expects you to choose one job for life anymore," she says. "Employers are looking for people who can learn quickly and work well with others. Those skills do not go out of date."

She also warns against following the crowd. When a job looks exciting on social media, thousands of young people rush towards it, and within a few years there are too many of them. Careers that look boring today, such as plumbing or nursing, may be the ones with the best pay and the most security in 2040.

Perhaps the best advice comes from Hoa's own story. She trained as an accountant, disliked it, worked in a bookshop for six years, and finally became a careers adviser at thirty-five. "Every job I did taught me something I use now," she says. "The path was not straight, but none of it was wasted."

questions.q: What is the main message of the passage?
options: Technology has created most of the jobs that exist today.
Students should train for jobs such as plumbing and nursing.
Since jobs keep changing, students should build skills that last rather than fix on one career.
Grandparents had fewer job choices than young people today.
questions.explanation: The passage moves from 'jobs are changing fast' to Hoa's advice: learn quickly, work with others, do not choose one job for life. Plumbing and nursing are just examples, and technology explains 'many but not all' of the new jobs.

questions.q: What did the employment website's report find about jobs advertised in Ho Chi Minh City?
options: Almost all of them were connected to technology.
Nearly a third had not existed in the same form in 2010.
Most of them were for delivery riders.
Nearly a third had not existed twenty years ago.
questions.explanation: The report compares today's jobs with 2010, not with twenty years ago, and says nearly a third did not exist 'in the same form'. Technology explains many, not almost all.

questions.q: Why does Hoa mention plumbing and nursing?
options: Because they are the jobs most young people rush towards.
Because she once worked in both of them.
Because unfashionable jobs may turn out to be the best paid and most secure.
Because they are likely to disappear by 2040.
questions.explanation: They are given as examples of careers that 'look boring today' but may offer 'the best pay and the most security in 2040' — the opposite of following the crowd.

questions.q: The phrase 'go out of date' in paragraph 3 is closest in meaning to
options: stop being useful
take a long time to learn
become too expensive
change their names
questions.explanation: Something that goes out of date is no longer useful or wanted. Hoa means that learning fast and working with others will always be needed.

questions.q: Why does the writer include Hoa's own story in the last paragraph?
options: To show that accountants are badly paid
To show that a career path can change direction without being wasted
To recommend working in a bookshop before choosing a career
To prove that Hoa made a serious mistake when she was young
questions.explanation: Her story ends with 'The path was not straight, but none of it was wasted' — a real-life example of the flexible attitude she recommends. She never calls her early choices a mistake.

questions.q: The work of delivery riders depends on a recently invented phone app.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says their work 'depends on a phone app that was invented only a few years ago'. True.

questions.q: Hoa left the bookshop because it closed down.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: We know she worked in a bookshop for six years and then became a careers adviser, but the passage gives no reason for leaving. Not Given.

passages.title: The Forests Under the Waves
passages.passage:
When people imagine a forest, they picture tall trees, birdsong and a floor covered with leaves. Very few think of the sea. Yet along many cold, rocky coasts, from California to South Africa to Japan, there are forests that grow entirely under water. They are made not of trees but of kelp, a giant brown seaweed that can grow half a metre in a single day and reach the height of a ten-storey building.

Kelp does not have roots. Instead, it holds onto rocks with a strong, hand-like part called a holdfast, and it rises towards the light with the help of small air-filled balls along its stem. From below, a kelp forest looks like a cathedral: long golden columns with sunlight moving between them.

These forests are home to an astonishing number of creatures. Small fish hide among the leaves from larger hunters. Sea urchins eat the kelp itself, and sea otters eat the urchins. This last relationship matters more than it sounds. In the 1800s, otters were hunted almost to extinction for their fur. With the otters gone, urchin numbers exploded, and whole kelp forests were eaten down to bare rock. Scientists call these empty areas 'urchin barrens'. When otters were protected and returned to the coast of California, the kelp slowly came back.

Kelp forests are also useful to people. They soften the force of waves, protecting beaches and harbours from storms. They take in carbon dioxide as they grow. And kelp is harvested for food and for a substance used in ice cream and toothpaste.

Today, however, kelp forests are shrinking in several parts of the world, mainly because warmer seas weaken the plants and encourage the animals that eat them. Some scientists are now replanting kelp by hand, much as foresters replant trees on land. It is slow work, but early results suggest that a forest under the waves, like one above them, can grow back if it is given the chance.

questions.q: Which of the following best summarises the passage?
options: Kelp forests are rich and useful ecosystems that are under threat but can recover.
Sea otters are the most important animals in the ocean.
Kelp is a valuable product used in food and toothpaste.
Warmer seas have destroyed most of the world's kelp forests.
questions.explanation: The passage describes what kelp forests are, who lives in them, why they matter and how they can come back. Otters and toothpaste are single details, and 'most' overstates the shrinking described in the last paragraph.

questions.q: How does kelp stay attached to the sea floor?
options: With deep roots that grow into the sand
With a hand-like part that grips the rocks
With air-filled balls along its stem
By wrapping its leaves around stones
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says kelp has no roots; it holds onto rocks with a 'holdfast'. The air-filled balls help it float upwards, not stay attached.

questions.q: What does the story of the sea otters show?
options: Otters eat kelp when there are no urchins left.
Sea urchins have now died out along the coast of California.
Removing one animal can change a whole underwater forest.
Hunting otters for fur is still common today.
questions.explanation: When the otters disappeared, urchins multiplied and ate whole forests; when otters returned, the kelp came back. One missing animal changed everything. The passage never says otters eat kelp or that urchins died out.

questions.q: The word 'exploded' in paragraph 3 is closest in meaning to
options: burst with a loud noise
increased very quickly
became dangerous
fell suddenly
questions.explanation: 'Urchin numbers exploded' means the urchin population grew very fast — so fast that whole forests were eaten. It has nothing to do with a real explosion.

questions.q: In paragraph 3, 'This last relationship' refers to
options: small fish hiding from larger hunters
sea urchins eating the kelp
sea otters eating the sea urchins
people hunting otters for fur
questions.explanation: The sentence before lists three feeding links; the last one mentioned is 'sea otters eat the urchins', and the rest of the paragraph explains why that link matters.

questions.q: Kelp forests are found only in warm tropical seas.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says they grow along 'cold, rocky coasts' and the last paragraph says warmer seas weaken them. So the statement is false.

questions.q: Most of the kelp harvested for food is eaten in Japan.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: The passage mentions that kelp is harvested for food and that Japan has kelp forests, but it never says where the food is eaten. Not Given.
